# Skill Description Budget: The 650-Character Ceiling and Silent Drop

On 2026-08-15, a repo-wide scan of `~/.claude/skills` found that **36 of 150 skills exceed the 650-character description ceiling** documented in `SkillSystem.md`, with a total description budget across the repo of **71,248 characters**. Per `SkillSystem.md`, an over-ceiling description causes the skill to be **silently dropped from the session listing — invisible and unroutable** — and this affects Claude Code, not only Codex. The scan also surfaced a documentation contradiction: `CreateSkill`'s own Gotchas section states the limit is 1024, not 650.

## Key Points

- **Worst offenders (characters):** Upgrade (1161), Art (1087), ContextSearch (1019), WriteStory (1015), CreateSkill (1008), Interceptor (1002), Hardening (1001). Thirty-six skills total exceed 650.
- **The failure is silent and total.** An over-ceiling skill is dropped from the session listing entirely — it cannot be routed to and produces no warning that it is missing. There is no degraded mode.
- **Unresolved doc conflict: 650 vs 1024.** `SkillSystem.md` documents a 650-character hard ceiling; `CreateSkill`'s Gotchas section says 1024. The conflict must be settled before any batch trim, since the two numbers imply very different remediation scopes.
- **`CreateSkill` supplies its own remediation template.** It had already solved its over-length problem the recommended way — cutting its description from 1022 to ~770 by moving enforcement prose into a `## Enforcement` body section rather than deleting content. The body is not budget-constrained; only the description is.
- **Six descriptions were trimmed and validated COMPLIANT** (single-line, under the 500-char recommendation, no forbidden arrays), but none of the six contains the mandatory `USE WHEN` keyword — verified pre-existing, not introduced by the trims, and queued as a separate pass.
- **A trim pass can silently lose trigger phrases.** A first attempt dropped 20 trigger phrases while claiming it had not; this was caught only by the Codex review gate, not by the trimming pass's own self-report.

## Details

The description budget is a context-efficiency constraint with a hard cliff rather than a gradual cost. Every skill's description is loaded into the session listing at startup, so 71,248 characters of descriptions across 150 skills is a fixed, always-paid tax on the context window — the same class of always-loaded overhead measured at ~21.5k tokens in [[concepts/session-context-footprint-audit]]. What distinguishes the description budget from ordinary context cost is the enforcement mechanism: rather than simply consuming tokens, an over-ceiling description removes the skill from routing entirely and without notice. A skill can therefore be present on disk, correctly authored, fully functional, and completely unreachable. This is the mirror image of the [[concepts/browser-automation-stack-audit-mac]] finding, where non-functional skills with assertive descriptions *win* routing; between them they establish that routing eligibility and actual capability are independent variables in both directions.

Two procedural lessons attach to this finding. The first is that the failure had already been documented before it was discovered empirically: the silent-drop behavior was rediscovered by experiment in Codex during the session when the answer was sitting in `SkillSystem.md` the whole time. The stated lesson — **check your own documentation before empirical rediscovery** — matters more in a system with 150 skills and multiple overlapping doc files than in a small one, because the cost of a doc read is trivially smaller than the cost of an experiment. The second is that the documentation itself cannot currently answer the question: `SkillSystem.md` says 650 and `CreateSkill` says 1024, so the batch-trim scope is undefined until the conflict is settled. Trimming 36 skills against the wrong number would either leave skills broken (if 650 is correct and 1024 was used) or destroy content unnecessarily (if the reverse).

The remediation pattern is already demonstrated in-repo. `CreateSkill` reduced its own description from 1022 to ~770 characters not by deleting information but by relocating enforcement prose into a `## Enforcement` section in the skill body, which is not subject to the description ceiling. This preserves the full instruction set for a skill that has been routed to while shrinking the always-loaded surface — precisely the "keep data retrievable but out of standing context" pattern documented in [[connections/keep-data-retrievable-but-out-of-standing-context]]. Trimming carries its own hazard, however: the first pass on six skills silently dropped 20 trigger phrases while reporting that it had not, and this was caught only by an independent Codex review gate. Trigger phrases are the routing signal, so losing them converts an over-ceiling skill (invisible) into an under-triggered one (visible but never selected) — a quieter version of the same failure. Any batch trim across the remaining 36 skills therefore needs a diff-level verification of trigger-phrase preservation, not a self-report from the trimming pass.

# SpeedProfiling Project (Baylor Football Velocity Profiling)

SpeedProfiling is a Baylor football velocity-profiling project that pulls full-game 10 Hz Catapult GPS data, aligns it with college football play-by-play (via CFBD / cfbfastR), and produces per-athlete speed/velocity profiles adapted from a workshop method authored by "Alex." The project is developed as a private R repository (`github.com/erash11/SpeedProfiling`, 176-package renv lockfile) executed against a 7-ticket implementation plan tracked in the KeystoneOS `.scratch/speedprofiling/issues/` directory, using the mattpocock `implement` and `code-review` skills. On 2026-07-18, tickets 01, 02, 04, and 07 were advanced; on 2026-07-20, ticket 05 (GPS↔play-by-play merge, on-field separation, workload tables) was closed and shipped on PR #3.

## Key Points

- **Ticket-driven, per-session workflow:** the project is decomposed into 7 tickets; each ticket is implemented in a fresh session via `/mattpocock-skills:implement <ticket path>`. The `Status:` line in each ticket file is the claim mechanism that prevents parallel-session collisions. Eric prefers fresh parallel sessions per ticket over driving all tickets from one session.
- **catapultR credentials-object API change:** the installed catapultR uses a new credentials-object API — `ofCloudCreateToken(sToken=…, sRegion='America')`; the old `token=` argument no longer exists. `R/01_get_data.R` was rewritten for this API in ticket 04.
- **Deleting a token file does not revoke it server-side:** the old 2023 Catapult token had to be revoked manually in the OpenField UI — removing the local JWT file does not invalidate the token on Catapult's servers. Ticket 02 hardened `.gitignore` against `AccessTokens.txt`/`*token*.txt` and migrated live values into `.Renviron`, but server-side revocation of a superseded token is a separate manual step (logged as an Eric-manual action item).
- **Full 10 Hz pull verified (ticket 04):** the pull retrieved 8,932,931 rows at true 10 Hz (0.1 s spacing, max velocity 20.3 mph) for all 61/61 athletes (79 MB, gitignored) plus 188 play-by-play plays; 69/69 testthat tests pass. A feasibility probe gate hard-stops before the bulk pull unless genuine 10 Hz rows with all required columns return.
- **Ticket 05 — GPS↔play-by-play alignment (2026-07-20):** merged 10 Hz GPS with play-by-play using the kickoff surge signature as a numerical time anchor, separated on-field from sideline athletes via a two-part rule (sideline boundary + metabolic-power gate), and produced per-play workload tables. Closed on PR #3. See [[concepts/speedprofiling-gps-playbyplay-alignment]].
- **Game selection is config, not code:** game selection moved from hardcoded `GAME_*` variables to a `GAMES` table in `R/config.R` (activity ID + cfbd args per row). Adding a game is a one-row config edit; an empty `GAMES` renders the activity list to pick from. Per-game `.rds` caching pays the slow pull once.
- **Stacked PRs merge in order #1 → #2 → #3;** ticket 04's PR #2 is stacked on ticket 03's PR #1.

## Details

The project adopts a set of workshop R scripts (from an author "Alex") as reference material and re-implements them ticket by ticket against Baylor's live data sources. Ticket 01 established the repo, adopted the Drive scripts/docs, and set FERPA rules in AGENTS.md with a CLAUDE.md adapter, gitignore protection, and a private repo. A standards review of the adopted scripts found four real defects — notably a timestamp-conversion bug in `01_get_data.R` and play-end windows in `02_combine_data.R` that erroneously absorb halftime gaps — which were logged to the tracker and mapped to downstream tickets 03–06 rather than patched twice in reference code. Ticket 02 decoded the Catapult JWT scopes (`connect, catapultr, sensor-read-only`, expiry 2126), confirming the sensor scope needed for the 10 Hz feasibility probe, and migrated tokens from an untracked `AccessTokens.txt` (hardened out via `.gitignore` patterns `AccessTokens.txt` and `*token*.txt`) into `C:\Users\eric_rash\Documents\.Renviron` (`CATAPULT_TOKEN`, `CFBD_API_KEY`). Two environment notes surfaced during setup: the local `G:\My Drive` mount is much faster for adopting workshop files than downloading them through the Drive API, and `reactablefmtr` was archived off CRAN so it must be installed from GitHub for a clean renv restore (the renv snapshot-type setting also had to be fixed for `renv::status()` to report clean).

Ticket 04 delivered the core game-data pull (8.9M rows at true 10 Hz for 61 athletes), verified end-to-end (69/69 tests, both `.rds` caches hit on re-run). The BYU game (BYU – G5 – 09.28.24) was auto-selected because ticket 02 had already verified its play-by-play and Eric was unavailable to pick interactively; swapping games is a one-row `GAMES` config edit. Ticket 04 anticipated two forward-looking findings for ticket 05: Catapult X/Y coordinates return in venue coordinates requiring a transform, and the cfbfastR `wallclock` column might simplify GPS↔play timestamp alignment. Ticket 05 (2026-07-20) resolved both — the venue-coordinate issue via PCA field-frame recovery and the timestamp alignment via the kickoff surge signature rather than `wallclock`. A recurring environment note: background R tasks can report a false "exit code 1" even when the script log shows a clean end-to-end run, so the log must be checked before assuming failure (see [[connections/background-task-exit-code-false-failure]]). Ticket 03 (analysis core + tests) and ticket 07 (KeystoneOS/SecondBrain integration) were also run as parallel fresh sessions, and ticket 06 (velocity profiles — sprint detection, NLS fits, bootstrap CIs, position-group comparisons) remains downstream.

message.content:
You are a knowledge compiler. Your job is to read a daily conversation log
and extract knowledge into structured wiki articles.

## Schema (AGENTS.md)

# AGENTS.md - Personal Knowledge Base Schema

> Adapted from [Andrej Karpathy's LLM Knowledge Base](https://gist.github.com/karpathy/442a6bf555914893e9891c11519de94f) architecture.
> Instead of ingesting external articles, this system compiles knowledge from your own AI conversations.

## The Compiler Analogy

```
daily/          = source code    (your conversations - the raw material)
LLM             = compiler       (extracts and organizes knowledge)
knowledge/      = executable     (structured, queryable knowledge base)
lint            = test suite     (health checks for consistency)
memlint         = test suite     (same, for the memory files loaded each session)
queries         = runtime        (using the knowledge)
```

You don't manually organize your knowledge. You have conversations, and the LLM handles the synthesis, cross-referencing, and maintenance.

---

## Architecture

### Layer 1: `daily/` - Conversation Logs (Immutable Source)

Daily logs capture what happened in your AI coding sessions. These are the "raw sources" - append-only, never edited after the fact.

```
daily/
├── 2026-04-01.md
├── 2026-04-02.md
├── ...
```

Each file follows this format:

```markdown
# Daily Log: YYYY-MM-DD

## Sessions

### Session (HH:MM) - Brief Title

**Context:** What the user was working on.

**Key Exchanges:**
- User asked about X, assistant explained Y
- Decided to use Z approach because...
- Discovered that W doesn't work when...

**Decisions Made:**
- Chose library X over Y because...
- Architecture: went with pattern Z

**Lessons Learned:**
- Always do X before Y to avoid...
- The gotcha with Z is that...

**Action Items:**
- [ ] Follow up on X
- [ ] Refactor Y when time permits
```

### Layer 2: `knowledge/` - Compiled Knowledge (LLM-Owned)

The LLM owns this directory entirely. Humans read it but rarely edit it directly.

```
knowledge/
├── index.md              # Master catalog - every article with one-line summary
├── log.md                # Append-only chronological build log
├── concepts/             # Atomic knowledge articles
├── connections/          # Cross-cutting insights linking 2+ concepts
└── qa/                   # Filed query answers (compounding knowledge)
```

### Layer 3: This File (AGENTS.md)

The schema that tells the LLM how to compile and maintain the knowledge base. This is the "compiler specification."

---

## Structural Files

### `knowledge/index.md` - Master Catalog

A table listing every knowledge article. This is the primary retrieval mechanism - the LLM reads this FIRST when answering any query, then selects relevant articles to read in full.

Format:

```markdown
# Knowledge Base Index

| Article | Summary | Compiled From | Updated |
|---------|---------|---------------|---------|
| [[concepts/supabase-auth]] | Row-level security patterns and JWT gotchas | daily/2026-04-02.md | 2026-04-02 |
| [[connections/auth-and-webhooks]] | Token verification patterns shared across Supabase auth and Stripe webhooks | daily/2026-04-02.md, daily/2026-04-04.md | 2026-04-04 |
```

### `knowledge/log.md` - Build Log

Append-only chronological record of every compile, query, and lint operation.

Format:

```markdown
# Build Log

## [2026-04-01T14:30:00] compile | Daily Log 2026-04-01
- Source: daily/2026-04-01.md
- Articles created: [[concepts/nextjs-project-structure]], [[concepts/tailwind-setup]]
- Articles updated: (none)

## [2026-04-02T09:00:00] query | "How do I handle auth redirects?"
- Consulted: [[concepts/supabase-auth]], [[concepts/nextjs-middleware]]
- Filed to: [[qa/auth-redirect-handling]]
```

---

## Article Formats

### Concept Articles (`knowledge/concepts/`)

One article per atomic piece of knowledge. These are facts, patterns, decisions, preferences, and lessons extracted from your conversations.

```markdown
---
title: "Concept Name"
aliases: [alternate-name, abbreviation]
tags: [domain, topic]
sources:
  - "daily/2026-04-01.md"
  - "daily/2026-04-03.md"
created: 2026-04-01
updated: 2026-04-03
---

# Concept Name

[2-4 sentence core explanation]

## Key Points

- [Bullet points, each self-contained]

## Details

[Deeper explanation, encyclopedia-style paragraphs]

## Related Concepts

- [[concepts/related-concept]] - How it connects

## Sources

- [[daily/2026-04-01.md]] - Initial discovery during project setup
- [[daily/2026-04-03.md]] - Updated after debugging session
```

### Connection Articles (`knowledge/connections/`)

Cross-cutting synthesis linking 2+ concepts. Created when a conversation reveals a non-obvious relationship.

```markdown
---
title: "Connection: X and Y"
connects:
  - "concepts/concept-x"
  - "concepts/concept-y"
sources:
  - "daily/2026-04-04.md"
created: 2026-04-04
updated: 2026-04-04
---

# Connection: X and Y

## The Connection

[What links these concepts]

## Key Insight

[The non-obvious relationship discovered]

## Evidence

[Specific examples from conversations]

## Related Concepts

- [[concepts/concept-x]]
- [[concepts/concept-y]]
```

### Q&A Articles (`knowledge/qa/`)

Filed answers from queries. Every complex question answered by the system can be permanently stored, making future queries smarter.

```markdown
---
title: "Q: Original Question"
question: "The exact question asked"
consulted:
  - "concepts/article-1"
  - "concepts/article-2"
filed: 2026-04-05
---

# Q: Original Question

## Answer

[The synthesized answer with [[wikilinks]] to sources]

## Sources Consulted

- [[concepts/article-1]] - Relevant because...
- [[concepts/article-2]] - Provided context on...

## Follow-Up Questions

- What about edge case X?
- How does this change if Y?
```

---

## Core Operations

### 1. Compile (daily/ -> knowledge/)

When processing a daily log:

1. Read the daily log file
2. Read `knowledge/index.md` to understand current knowledge state
3. Read existing articles that may need updating
4. For each piece of knowledge found in the log:
   - If an existing concept article covers this topic: UPDATE it with new information, add the daily log as a source
   - If it's a new topic: CREATE a new `concepts/` article
5. If the log reveals a non-obvious connection between 2+ existing concepts: CREATE a `connections/` article
6. UPDATE `knowledge/index.md` with new/modified entries
7. APPEND to `knowledge/log.md`

**Important guidelines:**
- A single daily log may touch 3-10 knowledge articles
- Prefer updating existing articles over creating near-duplicates
- Use Obsidian-style `[[wikilinks]]` with full relative paths from knowledge/
- Write in encyclopedia style - factual, concise, self-contained
- Every article must have YAML frontmatter
- Every article must link back to its source daily logs

### 2. Query (Ask the Knowledge Base)

1. Read `knowledge/index.md` (the master catalog)
2. Based on the question, identify 3-10 relevant articles from the index
3. Read those articles in full
4. Synthesize an answer with `[[wikilink]]` citations
5. If `--file-back` is specified: create a `knowledge/qa/` article and update index.md and log.md

**Why this works without RAG:** At personal knowledge base scale (50-500 articles), the LLM reading a structured index outperforms cosine similarity. The LLM understands what the question is really asking and selects pages accordingly. Embeddings find similar words; the LLM finds relevant concepts.

### 3. Lint (Health Checks)

Seven checks, run periodically:

1. **Broken links** - `[[wikilinks]]` pointing to non-existent articles
2. **Orphan pages** - Articles with zero inbound links from other articles
3. **Orphan sources** - Daily logs that haven't been compiled yet
4. **Stale articles** - Source daily log changed since article was last compiled
5. **Contradictions** - Conflicting claims across articles (requires LLM judgment)
6. **Missing backlinks** - A links to B but B doesn't link back to A
7. **Sparse articles** - Below 200 words, likely incomplete

Output: a markdown report with severity levels (error, warning, suggestion).

---

## Conventions

- **Wikilinks:** Use Obsidian-style `[[path/to/article]]` without `.md` extension
- **Writing style:** Encyclopedia-style, factual, third-person where appropriate
- **Dates:** ISO 8601 (YYYY-MM-DD for dates, full ISO for timestamps in log.md)
- **File naming:** lowercase, hyphens for spaces (e.g., `supabase-row-level-security.md`)
- **Frontmatter:** Every article must have YAML frontmatter with at minimum: title, sources, created, updated
- **Sources:** Always link back to the daily log(s) that contributed to an article

---

## Full Project Structure

```
llm-personal-kb/
|-- .claude/
|   |-- settings.json                # Hook configuration (auto-activates in Claude Code)
|-- .gitignore                       # Excludes runtime state, temp files, caches
|-- AGENTS.md                        # This file - schema + full technical reference
|-- README.md                        # Concise overview + quick start
|-- pyproject.toml                   # Dependencies (at root so hooks can find it)
|-- daily/                           # "Source code" - conversation logs (immutable)
|-- knowledge/                       # "Executable" - compiled knowledge (LLM-owned)
|   |-- index.md                     #   Master catalog - THE retrieval mechanism
|   |-- log.md                       #   Append-only build log
|   |-- concepts/                    #   Atomic knowledge articles
|   |-- connections/                 #   Cross-cutting insights linking 2+ concepts
|   |-- qa/                          #   Filed query answers (compounding knowledge)
|-- scripts/                         # CLI tools
|   |-- compile.py                   #   Compile daily logs -> knowledge articles
|   |-- query.py                     #   Ask questions (index-guided, no RAG)
|   |-- lint.py                      #   7 health checks (knowledge base)
|   |-- memlint.py                   #   6 health checks (memory tier)
|   |-- flush.py                     #   Extract memories from conversations (background)
|   |-- config.py                    #   Path constants
|   |-- utils.py                     #   Shared helpers
|-- hooks/                           # Claude Code hooks
|   |-- session-start.py             #   Injects knowledge into every session
|   |-- session-end.py               #   Extracts conversation -> daily log
|   |-- pre-compact.py               #   Safety net: captures context before compaction
|-- reports/                         # Lint reports (gitignored)
```

---

## Hook System (Automatic Capture)

Hooks are configured in `.claude/settings.json` and fire automatically when you use Claude Code in this project.

### `.claude/settings.json` Format

```json
{
  "hooks": {
    "SessionStart": [{ "matcher": "", "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "uv run python hooks/session-start.py", "timeout": 15 }] }],
    "PreCompact": [{ "matcher": "", "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "uv run python hooks/pre-compact.py", "timeout": 10 }] }],
    "SessionEnd": [{ "matcher": "", "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "uv run python hooks/session-end.py", "timeout": 10 }] }]
  }
}
```

Commands use simple relative paths from the project root. Empty `matcher` catches all events.

### Hook Details

**`session-start.py`** (SessionStart)
- Pure local I/O, no API calls, runs in under 1 second
- Reads `knowledge/index.md` and the most recent daily log
- Outputs JSON to stdout: `{"hookSpecificOutput": {"hookEventName": "SessionStart", "additionalContext": "..."}}`
- Claude sees the knowledge base index at the start of every session
- Max context: 20,000 characters

**`session-end.py`** (SessionEnd)
- Reads hook input from stdin (JSON with `session_id`, `transcript_path`, `cwd`)
- Copies the raw JSONL transcript to a temp file (no parsing in the hook - keeps it fast)
- Spawns `flush.py` as a fully detached background process
- Recursion guard: exits immediately if `CLAUDE_INVOKED_BY` env var is set

**`pre-compact.py`** (PreCompact)
- Same architecture as session-end.py
- Fires before Claude Code auto-compacts the context window
- Guards against empty `transcript_path` (known Claude Code bug #13668)
- Critical for long sessions: captures context before summarization discards it

**Why both PreCompact and SessionEnd?** Long-running sessions may trigger multiple auto-compactions before you close the session. Without PreCompact, intermediate context is lost to summarization before SessionEnd ever fires.

### Background Flush Process (`flush.py`)

Spawned by both hooks as a fully detached background process:
- **Windows:** `CREATE_NEW_PROCESS_GROUP | DETACHED_PROCESS` flags
- **Mac/Linux:** `start_new_session=True`

This ensures flush.py survives after Claude Code's hook process exits.

**What flush.py does:**
1. Sets `CLAUDE_INVOKED_BY=memory_flush` env var (prevents recursive hook firing)
2. Reads the pre-extracted conversation context from the temp `.md` file
3. Skips if context is empty or if same session was flushed within 60 seconds (deduplication)
4. Calls Claude Agent SDK (`query()` with `allowed_tools=[]`, `max_turns=2`)
5. Claude decides what's worth saving - returns structured bullet points or `FLUSH_OK`
6. Appends result to `daily/YYYY-MM-DD.md`
7. Cleans up temp context file
8. **End-of-day auto-compilation:** If it's past 6 PM local time (`COMPILE_AFTER_HOUR = 18`) and today's daily log has changed since its last compilation (hash comparison against `state.json`), spawns `compile.py` as another detached background process. This means compilation happens automatically once a day without needing a cron job or manual trigger.

### JSONL Transcript Format

Claude Code stores conversations as `.jsonl` files. Messages are nested under a `message` key:

```python
entry = json.loads(line)
msg = entry.get("message", {})
role = msg.get("role", "")     # "user" or "assistant"
content = msg.get("content", "")  # string or list of content blocks
```

Content can be a string or a list of blocks (`{"type": "text", "text": "..."}` dicts).

---

## Script Details

### compile.py - The Compiler

Uses the Claude Agent SDK's async streaming `query()`:

```python
async for message in query(
    prompt=compile_prompt,
    options=ClaudeAgentOptions(
        cwd=str(ROOT_DIR),
        system_prompt={"type": "preset", "preset": "claude_code"},
        allowed_tools=["Read", "Write", "Edit", "Glob", "Grep"],
        permission_mode="acceptEdits",
        max_turns=30,
    ),
):
```

- Builds a prompt with: AGENTS.md schema, current index, all existing articles, and the daily log
- Claude reads the daily log, decides what concepts to extract, and writes files directly
- `permission_mode="acceptEdits"` auto-approves all file operations
- Incremental: tracks SHA-256 hashes of daily logs in `state.json`, skips unchanged files
- Cost: ~$0.45-0.65 per daily log (increases as KB grows)

**CLI:**
```bash
uv run python scripts/compile.py              # compile new/changed only
uv run python scripts/compile.py --all        # force recompile everything
uv run python scripts/compile.py --file daily/2026-04-01.md
uv run python scripts/compile.py --dry-run
```

### query.py - Index-Guided Retrieval

Loads the entire knowledge base into context (index + all articles). No RAG.

At personal KB scale (50-500 articles), the LLM reading a structured index outperforms vector similarity. The LLM understands what you're really asking; cosine similarity just finds similar words.

**CLI:**
```bash
uv run python scripts/query.py "What auth patterns do I use?"
uv run python scripts/query.py "What's my error handling strategy?" --file-back
```

With `--file-back`, creates a Q&A article in `knowledge/qa/` and updates the index and log. This is the compounding loop - every question makes the KB smarter.

### lint.py - Health Checks

Seven checks:

| Check | Type | Catches |
|-------|------|---------|
| Broken links | Structural | `[[wikilinks]]` to non-existent articles |
| Orphan pages | Structural | Articles with zero inbound links |
| Orphan sources | Structural | Daily logs not yet compiled |
| Stale articles | Structural | Source logs changed since compilation |
| Missing backlinks | Structural | A links to B but B doesn't link back |
| Sparse articles | Structural | Under 200 words |
| Contradictions | LLM | Conflicting claims across articles |

**CLI:**
```bash
uv run python scripts/lint.py                    # all checks
uv run python scripts/lint.py --structural-only  # skip LLM check (free)
```

Reports saved to `reports/lint-YYYY-MM-DD.md`.

### memlint.py - Memory Tier Health Checks

`lint.py` stops at `knowledge/`. The files the harness actually injects into every
session live elsewhere and were never audited: `~/.claude/global-memory/` and the
active `~/.claude/projects/*/memory/` slugs. Drift there is the most expensive
drift in the system, because it is read at the start of every conversation.

Seven checks:

| Check | Type | Catches |
|-------|------|---------|
| Index drift | Structural | Memory file missing from MEMORY.md, or an index pointer with no file |
| Broken links | Structural | `[[links]]` that do not match any frontmatter `name:` in the slug |
| Name form | Structural | `name:` that is not the bare kebab stem (type belongs in `metadata.type`) |
| Near-duplicates | Structural | Within-slug TF-IDF similarity above the threshold |
| Cap overruns | Structural | A file past the character cap it declares in its own header |
| Content in index | Structural | Facts written into MEMORY.md, which is meant to hold pointers |
| Contradictions | LLM | Conflicting, redundant, or superseded claims across memory files |

**Scope.** Retired `C--Users-eric-rash*` slugs are excluded everywhere - the macOS
slugs were re-keyed from them, so including them reports history as duplication.
`handoffs/` and `transcripts/` are session records, not memory, and are never linted.
The LLM check defaults to `global-memory` + the `DEV` and `~` slugs, the ones that
load together in a working session; `--all-slugs` widens it.

**Similarity threshold.** Default 0.45. Measured 2026-09-01: the highest genuine
within-slug pair scored 0.33. The report always prints the top pairs per slug so
the number can be retuned against evidence.

**Report only.** memlint never edits a memory file. Merging and deleting memories
stays a human decision.

**CLI:**
```bash
uv run python scripts/memlint.py                    # all checks
uv run python scripts/memlint.py --structural-only  # skip LLM check (free)
uv run python scripts/memlint.py --all-slugs        # widen the LLM check
uv run python scripts/memlint.py --threshold 0.6    # retune near-duplicates
```

Reports saved to `reports/memlint-YYYY-MM-DD.md`; `--structural-only` writes
`memlint-YYYY-MM-DD-structural.md` instead, so a free run never clobbers the
day's paid-for LLM findings. Runs automatically after the Sunday 02:30
adjudication job.

---

## State Tracking

`scripts/state.json` tracks:
- `ingested` - map of daily log filenames to SHA-256 hashes, compilation timestamps, and costs
- `query_count` - total queries run
- `last_lint` - timestamp of most recent lint
- `last_memlint` - timestamp of most recent memory-tier lint
- `total_cost` - cumulative API cost

`scripts/last-flush.json` tracks flush deduplication (session_id + timestamp).

Both are gitignored and regenerated automatically.

---

## Dependencies

`pyproject.toml` (at project root):
- `claude-agent-sdk>=0.1.29` - Claude Agent SDK for LLM calls with tool use
- `python-dotenv>=1.0.0` - Environment variable management
- `tzdata>=2024.1` - Timezone data

## Customization

### Additional Article Types

Add directories like `people/`, `projects/`, `tools/` to `knowledge/`. Define the article format in this file (AGENTS.md) and update `utils.py`'s `list_wiki_articles()` to include them.

### Obsidian Integration

The knowledge base is pure markdown with `[[wikilinks]]` - works natively in Obsidian. Point a vault at `knowledge/` for graph view, backlinks, and search.

### Scaling Beyond Index-Guided Retrieval

At ~2,000+ articles / ~2M+ tokens, the index becomes too large for the context window. At that point, add hybrid RAG (keyword + semantic search) as a retrieval layer before the LLM. See Karpathy's recommendation of `qmd` by Tobi Lutke for search at scale.

# A Closeout With Nothing to Commit Is a Verification Result

The 21:52 closeout on 2026-10-10 found every `~/DEV` repository already clean and pushed from earlier sessions, made no new commits, and recorded that explicitly: "None this session." Its output was a set of verified negatives — no uncommitted or unpushed work anywhere, registry drift stable at 14 items with no new drift introduced, the landed ledger unchanged at 157 files in the last day, and the 7 `.errors.log` entries confirmed as carried over from prior days rather than newly generated. The session signed off on the judgment that the error log is "informational, not a git blocker." A concurrent closeout on the same evening reached the opposite disposition for `~/.claude`, holding 1,892 dirty files rather than committing them — showing that "nothing to commit" is a per-repository finding, not a global state.

## Key Points

- **A zero-change closeout is a complete result, not a skipped one,** provided the checks actually ran: clean working trees, no unpushed commits, an unchanged landed count, and drift confirmed stable rather than merely unexamined.
- **"No new drift" is a stronger statement than "drift exists."** Holding the count at 14 across a working day establishes that the day's activity did not worsen the registry, which is what makes deferring reconciliation defensible.
- **The error-log entries were classified rather than cleared,** each attributed to a cause outside the harness — the compiler backlog, the memsearch index, `gps-pull` API failures, and the digest send — so none could be closed by a git action.
- **Open decisions were carried forward with owners and counts:** 8 across two repos (6 in `SportScienceResearchRepo`, 2 in `Flint`), covering the concierge pilot, Batch 80, an Evans entry, and interview prep.
- **The 7-day staleness clock was reported per project with ages** — `NCAA_BestPractices_Doc` at 1 day, `HPI_Protocol`, `Education_Curriculum`, and `cmj-traffic-light` at 2 days each — converting a vague "these are going cold" into a dated watch list.
- **A clean verdict in one closeout does not generalise across repositories.** The parallel agent-session closeout held `~/.claude` with 1,892 dirty files pending a privacy and sync review, so the day ended with both a clean sign-off and an unresolved hold.

## Details

The value of recording a nothing-happened closeout lies in the difference between a check that ran and found nothing and a check that never ran. The two states are indistinguishable from the absence of output, which is the general failure mode behind reading quiet as health. By stating which repositories were walked, what the landed count was, and that the error entries predate the session, the closeout converts silence into a positive negative result that a later reader can rely on. This mirrors the logic of a compile run that produced zero articles: the backlog was cleared and a dated judgment of "nothing durable" was recorded, which is a different artifact from no compile at all.

The error-log handling is the session's main substantive judgment. Seven entries persisted, and rather than clearing them to silence the session-start banner, the closeout classified each as requiring a fix outside the harness and explicitly declined to treat them as a blocker to signing off. That is the correct resolution of a genuine tension: `.errors.log` functions both as a work queue and as a nag, and clearing it early would have converted a record of unresolved conditions into a record of conditions someone intended to resolve. The same day's selective-clearing precedent — clear fixed entries, keep unfixed ones — is the finer-grained version of this move, but it requires knowing which entries are fixed; here the memsearch rebuild's verification had not yet run, so none qualified.

The staleness and open-decision reporting is the other durable output. Both are lists the session could not act on — a decision has an owner who is not the agent, and a stale project needs a step that is real work rather than closeout work — so the honest disposition is to surface them with enough specificity to be actionable next time. Reporting `NCAA_BestPractices_Doc` at 1 day alongside three projects at 2 days is more useful than a count of four stale projects, because the ages say which one will trip the rule first.

A caveat follows from the day's parallelism. Three closeout-flavoured sessions ran at 21:52 against overlapping state, and they did not agree: one found every `~/DEV` repo clean, one held `~/.claude` pending review of 1,892 files, and a third was mid-consolidation on a full `MEMORY.md`. "Nothing to commit" was therefore an accurate report of the repositories that session walked and not a statement about the machine. A clean closeout should name its scope for exactly this reason — the same discipline that keeps a closeout from absorbing another session's work also keeps its clean verdict from overclaiming.

# DEV Project Migration to GitHub + Google Drive (Destination-Split Policy)

On 2026-09-14, a staged full-DEV migration moved all Codex and Claude projects to durable remote storage, governed by a destination-split policy that routes each artifact type to GitHub, Google Drive, or neither based on sensitivity and size. The audit at migration start counted 142 local repos with `erash11` remotes, 144 GitHub repos (141 private / 3 public), and none ahead of remote; Google Drive was mounted at `G:\My Drive` with `_DRIVE` mapping to `00_Primary_Storage_Drive`. On 2026-09-24 the policy entered an operational phase: the S2 evaluation data was migrated to Drive and a Parquet-snapshot exchange layer was stood up so two machines could share data without reaching into each other's live working trees.

## Key Points

- **Destination split by artifact type:** code / docs / `AGENTS.md` / `STATUS.md` → GitHub; large datasets, vendor exports, installers, and proprietary files → Google Drive; athlete-identifiable or health data → Drive only (never GitHub); raw conversation transcripts → Drive backup (never in project repos); credentials and `.env` files → neither destination; sanitized memory and handoff summaries → private GitHub context repos.
- **Working repos stay local:** live Git working directories remain under `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV`. Google Drive holds external data and archives, not live working repos.
- **Intentional public/local exceptions:** `Travel_Map`, `SportScienceResearchRepo`, and `JumpReporting` remain intentionally public; `DexaProject` stays local/Drive-only due to sensitive athlete data and is never pushed to GitHub.
- **Codex history not durably backed up:** Codex conversation history is preserved locally under `C:\Users\eric_rash\.codex\sessions\` but is NOT in GitHub and NOT independently backed up off-device — a remaining gap.
- **Raw backups are themselves sensitive:** raw conversation backups contain athlete names, medical context, and historical credentials, so the Drive archive must stay private and unshared — the backup inherits the sensitivity of the most sensitive content it captures.
- **Snapshot exchange, not live cross-reads (2026-09-24):** each pull repo runs `export_snapshot.py` to emit Parquet snapshots that the other machine consumes; the Mac rsyncs `ol_scores.csv` and `team_scores.csv` from `~/DEV/S2_Evaluation/data/` into the Drive S2 folder, and Perch's Windows reads are queued to be repointed at the snapshots rather than at live sources.
- **The Drive-only rule is enforced at the tool layer, and that costs verifiability (2026-09-24):** a direct listing of the S2 Drive folder was refused because the listing itself contains an athlete-named file, leaving the migration's arrival unconfirmed rather than verified.

## Details

The migration's governing principle is that destination is a function of both size and sensitivity, not a single default. Ordinary code and documentation flow to GitHub where version history and collaboration matter; bulky or proprietary binaries (datasets, vendor exports, installers) go to Google Drive to keep repositories lean; and anything athlete-identifiable or health-related is confined to Drive-only storage so it never enters a Git remote at all. Credentials and `.env` files are excluded from both remotes entirely. Sanitized memory and handoff summaries occupy a fourth lane — private GitHub "context repos" — allowing durable, version-controlled continuity documents without exposing raw sensitive material. This mirrors the athlete-data-stays-local convention already established in Baylor's sports-tech pipelines (see [[concepts/kinexon-volleyball-tracking-project]] and [[concepts/speedprofiling-velocity-project]]), where `data/` directories are gitignored so athlete-level data never leaves the machine.

Seven remaining Claude Cowork projects (S2 Cognition, WebApps, PlayerProfiles, StaffProject_BE, Post Season Analysis, UPskilling, PersonalKnowledgeManagement) were queued for migration via a `/migrate-project-to-disk` command and later reported complete in a resume checkpoint pending verification. Several follow-ups remained open: confirming that `Ath_Medicine`, `Baylor_Exposure_Data`, and `Risk_Stratification_Engine` contain no identifiable athlete/health data before their GitHub state is trusted; resolving `_INBOX` changes (a modified `recv.py`, two untracked closeout scripts, and five recovered Python utilities from `agent-skills/_recovered-from-codex/`); a guarded Windows skills v2 sync blocked on an absent `.sync-v2-ready` marker with divergent agent/Codex skill copies to reconcile; and stale documentation (`_INBOX/docs/STATUS.md` still claiming 7 Cowork projects remain, and a stale root "36 `.from-windows` files" item). Optional cleanup included removing a 3.2 GB `C:\Users\eric_rash\Documents\Codex` scratch folder and duplicate clones under `Desktop\DEV\_to_delete\2026-09-14_dup_clones`. Key final commits: DEV router `847bfb9`, `_INBOX` migration handoff `c7e0326`, Claude config `9e807eb`, global memory `b59bf55`, recovered agent utilities `4e00e86`.

The 2026-09-24 machine-split day exercised the policy in two instructive ways. First, once data lives on Drive rather than in a repo, two machines working the same projects need a defined exchange format; the answer adopted was per-repo `export_snapshot.py` runs producing Parquet snapshots, with each host reading the committed snapshot instead of the other host's live data — a read-only, reproducible handoff that keeps the Drive copy authoritative and avoids the divergence problems that plague direct cross-machine reads. Second, the Drive-only rule for athlete data proved to be enforced mechanically and more broadly than the written policy suggests: the permission layer refused a mere *directory listing* of the S2 folder because athlete names appear in file names, meaning identifiable data lives in the metadata as well as the payload (see [[concepts/athlete-data-permission-block]]). No workaround was attempted, so the cost was accepted as an explicit verification gap in the day's handoff — the guardrail behaving correctly, at the price of not being able to confirm from that session that the migration landed.

# DEV Sync 2026-09-22: Union-Merge Transcripts, Manifest Non-Discovery, and Cross-Machine Memory

A `/dev-sync` run on 2026-09-22 walked 146 repositories to bring the Mac in line with GitHub: two pulled (`_INBOX`, `DataBase_GPS_Reporting`), one pushed (`CommandCentre`), one cloned (`TOS_Evidence_Brief`, created on Windows 9/21), with 22 active and 117 dormant-and-clean, and no conflicts. Its durable findings concern how recurring cross-machine friction is resolved: a merge strategy for append-only logs, a manifest that does not discover its own new inputs, and the fact that Tier A memory does not travel between machines. The transcript-merge finding was already established on 2026-09-16 and recurred again on 2026-09-24, making it a three-instance pattern; the manifest gap recurred on 9/24 and again on 9/29.

## Key Points

- **Union merge is the right strategy for append-only transcript logs.** Mac/Windows conflicts in `global-memory/transcripts/*.md` resolve cleanly by keeping every line from both machines, producing no `.from-*` files to clean up afterward.
- **The same resolution was reached independently on 2026-09-16**, where `global-memory` transcript-log conflicts were settled by keeping both sides rather than picking a winner, again with no `.from-*` files created — before the merge strategy was configured.
- **The manual form is to delete only the conflict markers.** On 2026-09-24 two clashing transcript logs (9/23 and 9/24) were resolved exactly this way — text from both sides kept, only the `<<<<<<<`/`=======`/`>>>>>>>` lines removed — confirming that for this artifact class there is nothing to adjudicate.
- **The union strategy is class-specific, not general.** On 2026-09-29 a conflict on the router file `~/DEV/RESEARCH.md` was a *duplicate* `Flint` entry added independently by both machines, and the correct resolution was to drop one line — a union would have listed the project twice.
- **The backup manifest does not auto-discover new repos.** `TOS_Evidence_Brief` — created on Windows the previous day — was absent from `~/.claude/scripts/backup-manifest.json`, which made the 09:05 backup report an error. Adding it fixed the report (prior file at `backup-manifest.json.bak-2026-09-22`). On 2026-09-24 the identical class reappeared as `manifest-unmanaged:RunningTheRoom`, and the same entry was still outstanding on 2026-09-29.
- **Tier A memory does not cross machines.** Durable GPS decisions were therefore written into the repo's own `docs/STATUS.md` *and* `global-memory/MEMORY.md` so the Windows machine would see them.
- **A folder name containing a space (`DEV/Linda Projects`) broke a sync step again** and had to be redone with the path quoted — a recurrence of the same hazard seen on 2026-09-11.
- **`compile.py` was deliberately not run.** A compile costs ~$1.28, so clearing the memory-compiler backlog was left as the user's call; the warning persists in `.errors.log` until then, and had grown to 3 logs behind by 2026-09-24.

## Details

The union-merge finding names a resolution strategy that fits the artifact's semantics rather than a generic "take one side" rule. A transcript log is append-only and each machine appends independently, so the two versions are not competing revisions of the same content — they are disjoint additions to a shared record. Under that structure the correct merge keeps every line, and the usual conflict-file machinery (`.from-*` copies awaiting manual adjudication) is pure overhead because there is nothing to adjudicate. The pattern now has three independent confirmations arriving by different routes: a hand resolution on 9/16 that consciously declined to pick a winner, a configured merge driver on 9/22, and a purely mechanical marker-strip on 9/24. That an unaided human judgment, a configured strategy, and a mechanical cleanup all converge on identical output is the strongest available evidence that the strategy matches the artifact rather than the tooling — and it argues that the merge driver should have been configured after the first instance rather than the second. This is the same classify-by-kind-before-resolving discipline applied in [[concepts/cross-machine-conflict-file-triage]], where treating accumulating records as revisions would have discarded 324 unique forecast-log rows, and the accumulate-versus-supersede distinction generalized in [[connections/newer-is-not-more-complete]]. Notably, the 9/22 PFF loader bug was the identical error one layer down — a replace where a merge was required.

The 2026-09-29 `RESEARCH.md` conflict is the boundary case that keeps the union strategy honest. Both machines had independently added a router entry for the new `Flint` project, so the conflict was concurrent agreement rather than disagreement — and the correct resolution was to keep one line and drop the other, because a router index is a set keyed by project identity rather than an append-only sequence. Applying the transcript strategy there would have produced a doubled entry. The practical rule, developed in [[concepts/router-index-duplicate-entry-merge]] and synthesised across all four observed artifact classes in [[connections/classify-the-conflict-by-the-artifacts-kind]], is that a merge strategy is correct only for the class it was derived from, and that a conflict on the `~/DEV` router files should be read as an expected duplicate rather than investigated as a mangled file.

The manifest gap is a recurrence rather than a novelty, and its recurrence is the point. A repo created on one machine does not announce itself to a backup manifest maintained on another; the manifest's coverage is declared, not discovered, so a new repo is invisible to it until a human adds a line. The 09:05 backup error was in this case an honest signal — the manifest check did fire — but the general hazard is the one catalogued in [[connections/silent-omission-defeats-per-stage-success]] and [[connections/aggregate-success-hides-a-shrunken-work-set]]: every managed item succeeds while the unmanaged item is never counted. Prior instances at [[concepts/backup-manifest-coverage-gap-2026-09-09]] and [[concepts/dev-folder-manifest-default-deny]], the `Claude outputs` complaint resolved on 9/16 by relocation rather than by a manifest entry ([[concepts/dev-folder-is-not-a-document-store]]), the `manifest-unmanaged:RunningTheRoom` entry two days after this run, and that same entry still outstanding a further five days later ([[concepts/carried-forward-maintenance-residue-2026-09-29]]), put the count well past the threshold at which — by the reasoning in [[connections/fix-the-generator-not-the-artifacts]] — the fix belongs in the discovery mechanism rather than in yet another manual manifest edit. Each individual fix is a one-line change, which is precisely why the structural fix keeps getting deferred.

The Tier A observation is a routing constraint with immediate practical force. Tier A memory is local to the machine that wrote it, so any decision that a second machine must honor — here, that the Mac owns the pulls and the Windows GPS writer is stopped — cannot live there alone. Writing it into the repository's `docs/STATUS.md` puts it in a location git already replicates, and mirroring it into `global-memory/MEMORY.md` reaches the synced memory surface; between them the decision arrives on the other machine by two independent paths. This extends the content-to-tier routing matrix in [[concepts/claude-code-memory-architecture]] with a cross-machine axis, and matches the working-machine-authors-the-fix pattern in [[concepts/fix-from-the-working-machine-handoff]]. Finally, the deliberate refusal to run `compile.py` is a recorded non-action rather than an oversight: a ~$1.28 spend is a user decision, so the backlog warning was left standing in `.errors.log` with the command documented in the compiler's README — consistent with treating `.errors.log` as an escalation channel that clears only on a verified clean run.

# Closeout Gaps: Touched Repos Without STATUS Updates and Checks That Did Not Run

The 2026-10-13 closeouts on the Mac surfaced two kinds of incompleteness that a clean-looking closeout can hide. One was a repo that was touched during the day but whose `docs/STATUS.md` was not updated, a gap against the rule that every touched repo gets a STATUS update. The other was a verification step that was part of the closeout but whose script was not on disk, so it did not run. Across the day's closeouts, the handling also showed how to commit files written by another session without mixing them into this session's commits.

## Key Points

- **The STATUS rule applies to every repo touched, not only the one that was the focus.** The earlier closeout found no STATUS change in any repo, although Flint had been touched, so the gap was recorded as an action item.
- **A missing check must be reported as not run.** `skill-portability-check.py` was absent, so the closeout did not run it, and the closeout said so instead of implying the check passed.
- **Uncommitted files from another session get their own commit.** Flint had 101 changed files written by another session. They were committed as one separate commit, `9eede18`, and named in the report so their source stayed clear.
- **Push results need a second read.** After a push, the branch status showed "one commit ahead," which meant the push had not finished. The check was repeated before the closeout was called clean.
- **Edits that match a duplicated heading fail, so insert under the first match.** In `ZoteroInjestion/STATUS.md` the heading "Current state" appeared twice, and an edit keyed on it failed until the new line was placed under the first heading.

## Details

The first closeout of the day established the gap with a simple test: a repo that was worked in during the session should show a changed STATUS file. Flint was worked in, and its STATUS was not changed, so the closeout could not honestly say every touched repo had been recorded. The action item asks for the STATUS update in Flint and a decision on whether the closeout should check each touched repo by name rather than relying on memory of what was touched. The same pattern appeared earlier in the week in closeouts that reported clean while a foreign change was still in the tree, so the sign-off is only as wide as the surface that was actually walked.

The second closeout handled the Flint changes as a deliberate scope decision. The files were not written in the closing session, so mixing them into that session's commits would have made the history misleading. Committing them as a separate commit, and naming them in the report, keeps authorship legible while still leaving the repo clean. This differs from leaving foreign work untouched, because here the files were already staged book text with no secrets or databases, and pushing them was the owner's intent. The distinction turns on whether the other session's output is complete and safe, which the closeout checked before committing.

# Branch Drift Hides Working Code From main

A cleanup of `~/.claude/claude-memory-compiler` deleted nine merged branches and, in the process, exposed a more serious condition: **`main` was not what was running.** The backfill feature used to recover a dead flush existed only on a branch, so for 17 days a working capability was absent from the mainline and invisible to anything that read `main`. The same sweep found five other repositories parked on feature branches in the same state, and found that the closeout routine had a blind spot that let the condition persist unreported.

## Key Points

- **Nine merged branches were deleted after each was verified at 0 commits not in `main`** — including `session-start-progressive-disclosure`, merged that same day. Nothing was lost. The accompanying rule: if a delete is ever refused, stop and report, never force.
- **A branch holding working code keeps `main` lying about the project's capability.** The flush-recovery backfill was real, tested, and unreachable from `main` for 17 days.
- **The closeout sweep never checked `~/.claude/claude-memory-compiler`.** It walked `~/DEV` plus three config repos, which is why past closeouts signed off "clear" over an unmerged branch. Fixed in this session; the sweep now covers nested `~/.claude` repos (149 repos swept).
- **Five repositories remain parked on feature branches** — `AgentAssist`, `PT_Dash`, `Football/SpeedProfiling`, `CFB_Analytics_Lab`, `ZoteroInjestion` — all pushed and clean, but carrying the same `main`-drift that was just fixed in the compiler.
- **A branch named `origin` in an earlier ref listing was a listing artifact, not a real branch** — one more case of a tool's output needing interpretation before action.

## Details

The deletion half of this work was routine and the finding half was not. Verifying each branch at zero commits not in `main` before deleting is the correct order of operations, and it is what made the sweep safe; the standing rule that a refused delete must be reported rather than forced keeps the safety property intact under surprise. But the question that produced the real result was not about branches at all — a question about one log line (`Indexed 0 chunks`) that turned out to be correct behaviour nonetheless exposed five distinct problems when pulled on, including the branch drift itself, a leftover backup folder containing raw session text that needed gitignoring, and an SDK pinned at 0.2.136 while `main` already expected 0.2.152.

The structural lesson concerns what a sweep's *scope* implies. The closeout routine reported "clear to sign off" repeatedly while an unmerged branch sat in a repository the sweep did not visit, which means the verdict was locally truthful and globally wrong — the same shape as a backup reporting OK while the SSD it would have copied to was unmounted, or a manifest-driven job succeeding over a folder it never enumerated. A sweep's clean verdict carries exactly as much assurance as its enumeration is complete, and the fix here was to widen the enumeration to nested `~/.claude` repositories rather than to change any check. The five remaining parked repositories are the known residual, and naming them converts an invisible condition into a work queue.

The branch-drift condition has a timing remedy established elsewhere in this knowledge base: open the pull request the same day, because otherwise the next sync reports the project's state from `main` and understates it. The compiler's 17 days is the long-tail version of the 38-commit `step1-triage` stranding, and both show that the cost is not paid once at discovery but continuously, every time a tool reads the mainline tip.

# Milvus Lite Version Skew Corrupts the memsearch Index

On 2026-10-10 the `daily-backup` job failed its `memsearch-index:full-set` step with the error "database was made by an older Milvus Lite version." Seventy-one other jobs completed; only the index step failed, and an independently running index process (pid 44870) ran ~29 minutes before exiting with the same error. The chosen remedy was to move `~/.memsearch/milvus.db` aside as `milvus.db.pre-3x-2026-10-10` and rebuild from scratch, on the grounds that the index is derived from markdown notes and therefore loses nothing. The rebuild indexed 14,614 chunks and exited 0.

## Key Points

- **The failure is version skew in a local database file, not corruption of source data.** A Milvus Lite upgrade left an on-disk database the new library refuses to open, and because the index is derived from markdown notes, discarding and rebuilding is the cheapest correct fix.
- **Move aside rather than delete.** The old database was renamed `milvus.db.pre-3x-2026-10-10`, keeping a rollback path and a dated record of what the pre-upgrade state was. An earlier plan named it `milvus.db.bak-2026-10-10`; the `.pre-3x-` form is what was actually run.
- **A rebuild must cover the full path set.** A partial path set is destructive — indexing a subset deletes previously indexed data. The full set is 13 paths, of which 12 exist (`~/.codex/memories` does not), and this constraint was already recorded in memory.
- **Two concurrent index runs contend for the same database lock,** so a duplicate run has to be stopped and the existing one allowed to finish; this is the same lock-contention signature previously seen as an exit-1 after a long wait.
- **The `dcg` guard blocked the agent's own `mv` of a path under `~`,** so the move had to be run by the user with a `!` prefix; separately, the guard blocked shell-variable redirects, and literal absolute paths in the memsearch invocation passed. No `settings.json` change was made.
- **Verification is a positive log line, not the absence of an error:** confirm the next `daily-backup` run (or a hand run of `daily-backup.ps1`) shows the `INDEX full set` step passing before archiving and clearing `.errors.log`. As of the 21:52 closeout this verification had not yet happened, and the error log still carried 7 entries.
- **The backup's own exit code is not evidence the SSD leg ran.** A parallel session recorded that `status: OK` does not establish the CRASHBOX volume was mounted and copied — the check is the receipt file at `/Volumes/CRASHBOX/AssistantBackup/_receipts/run-*.txt`, because rsync preserves source mtimes and so `ls -la` or `du` on the destination shows week-old dates even after a perfect capture.

## Details

This is a textbook instance of install-time environment capture rotting: a library upgrade changed the reader while the written artifact stayed at the old format, and nothing surfaced until a scheduled job happened to touch it. What makes the diagnosis tractable is the derived/primary distinction — the Milvus database holds no information that does not exist in the markdown notes it was built from, so the decision tree collapses to "rebuild" rather than "migrate" or "recover." Recognizing that an artifact is regenerable is what licenses the destructive-looking move; the same reasoning that made interim publication cheap in the open-data case applies here to deleting four hours of indexing work. The rename rather than delete is still worth the keystrokes, because it costs nothing and preserves the ability to answer "what did the old file actually contain" if the rebuild turns out to have missed a path.

Two operational hazards surfaced around the rebuild rather than in it. The first is that the rebuild's correctness depends on its argument list: memsearch treats the supplied path set as authoritative, so indexing a subset silently drops everything outside it. That turns a convenient "just reindex the one folder that changed" into a data-loss operation, and it is why the full 13-path list (12 existing) was reconstructed from memory before the run. The second is lock contention. Two index processes against one database produce a stall whose externally visible form — a long wait, then a nonzero exit — is indistinguishable from a crash, which is exactly the signature previously catalogued for `memsearch-drain.ps1`. The correct first check on a long-running index is therefore "is another run already holding the lock," not "is the code broken."

The `dcg` guard's behavior is worth recording precisely because the session chose not to weaken it. The guard refuses any agent-issued `mv` of a path under the home directory and refuses shell-variable redirects, which meant the single necessary move had to be handed to the user as a `!`-prefixed command — the narrowest-sufficient escalation rather than a settings edit. The agent initially proposed relaxing the guard for the one move and then abandoned that route when it proved unnecessary. Literal absolute paths inside the memsearch call were accepted, which is the workaround that kept the rebuild itself agent-runnable. No change was made to `settings.json`, keeping the guard intact for every subsequent session; this is the same posture taken when a dcg rule blocked branch deletion and a multi-repo status loop.

A final verification lesson arrived from a concurrent stack-health session on the same evening. That session deferred the Milvus rebuild in favour of fixing git divergence and a full `MEMORY.md`, and in the process established that the nightly backup's `OK` status says nothing about whether the SSD leg actually ran — the receipt file under `/Volumes/CRASHBOX/AssistantBackup/_receipts/` is the only artifact that dates the capture, because rsync's mtime preservation makes the destination directory listing look stale regardless. That is the same shape as the index failure itself: a status field whose scope is narrower than the question being asked of it, answered correctly only by finding the artifact that the operation authored.

# Handoff Document Placement: Never Write to /tmp

On 2026-08-15, a session resuming work on the portfolio board project could not locate its handoff document. A search of the entire home directory — six levels deep, excluding `Library` and `node_modules` — turned up nothing. The file had been written by the prior session to `/tmp/`, which is invisible to a home-directory search and is wiped on reboot. The handoff was copied to `/Users/kristinarash/DEV/project-triage/handoff-portfolio-board-task4-2026-08-15.md`, establishing the rule that handoff documents belong in the project directory.

## Key Points

- **`/tmp/` is doubly wrong for handoffs:** the file does not survive a reboot, and it is outside the search path a fresh session would naturally check (a home-directory sweep). Either failure alone loses the document; together they make the loss silent.
- **Write handoffs into the project directory.** The recovered file now lives at `/Users/kristinarash/DEV/project-triage/`, alongside the work it describes, where both a filesystem search and a repository listing will find it.
- **When a handoff cannot be found, ask the user for the *project name*, not the file path.** The project name is something the user reliably knows and it localizes the search immediately; a path the user must reconstruct from memory is slower and often wrong.
- **A near-limit session should not start work it cannot finish.** Task 4 was deliberately not begun: it requires spawning implementer and reviewer subagents over a long run, and the usage limit was close. Starting and being cut off mid-run was judged worse than not starting at all.
- **State at handoff:** Tasks 1–3 done, pushed, 59 tests passing. Work happens in the worktree `~/DEV/project-triage/.claude/worktrees/portfolio-merge-editor`, not the main folder. Task 4 is to make `save_registry` atomic (temp-file write plus swap), with code and two regression tests already specified in the plan file. Tasks 5–10 follow the same one-subagent-per-task loop; the final merge to `master` has a known conflict requiring a user decision.

## Details

The failure mode here is specific to ephemeral system directories and is worth stating precisely: a handoff document's entire purpose is to survive the boundary between sessions, so writing it to a location defined by the operating system as not surviving boundaries defeats it categorically. `/tmp` is an attractive default for an agent writing a scratch file — it is always writable and requires no decision about where the file belongs — but a handoff is not scratch output. The recovery in this case depended on the user having the prior session's tool output available to paste; without that, the file's location was unrecoverable by search, because the search space a fresh session reasons about is the home directory and the project tree, not the system temp directory. The generalizable rule is that any artifact whose value is realized in a *later* session must be written where a later session will look, which in practice means the project directory or a durable notes location — the same reasoning that put the machine-restore handoff into a committed `~/.claude/global-memory/handoffs/` path in [[concepts/machine-restore-closeout-handoff]] rather than anywhere transient.

The retrieval lesson is a small but reusable debugging heuristic. When a search for a named file fails, the instinct is to widen the search or ask the user to confirm the filename. Both are slow: widening a home-directory sweep costs time and still misses `/tmp`, and a user asked for a file path will frequently supply an approximation. Asking instead for the *project name* changes the query from "where is this file" to "which tree should I be looking in," which the user can answer immediately and correctly, and which usually collapses the search to a single directory. This applies whenever an identifier the user owns (project, feature, ticket) can substitute for an identifier the machine owns (path, hash, filename).

The decision not to begin Task 4 records a judgment about work granularity under a resource ceiling. The task's shape — spawning implementer and reviewer subagents, per the two-stage review methodology in [[concepts/subagent-driven-development]] — means it consumes a long, uninterruptible run rather than decomposing into resumable increments. With the usage limit near, the two options were an unstarted task with a clean handoff, or a half-executed task whose partial state would need to be understood and possibly unwound by the next session. Choosing the former treats a clean boundary as more valuable than marginal progress, which is the correct trade when the work's own structure resists being resumed midway. It also parallels the closeout classification in [[concepts/machine-restore-closeout-handoff]], where items were sorted into finished, self-draining, and deliberately parked rather than all being pushed toward completion.

# Mac-Owned GPS/Perch/VALD Pulls and Sleep-Induced Lateness

On 2026-09-21 the three Baylor athlete-data pulls — GPS (Catapult), Perch/PlayerProfiles, and VALD/ForcePlate — were moved off the Windows laptop and onto the Mac, and the same evening's closeout session verified the first afternoon of Mac-owned scheduled runs. All three exited 0 and carried data through 9/21, but two of the three finished roughly an hour late because the Mac was asleep at their scheduled time. The eventual decision, reached the following morning, was to accept the lateness rather than force a daily wake, on the grounds that the data arrived and only its arrival time was unreliable.

## Key Points

- **Schedule:** GPS 10:00 / 16:30, Perch 10:05 / 16:35, VALD 10:10 / 16:40 — all three now Mac-owned. The Windows scheduled task still fires at 8 PM but pulls nothing; see [[concepts/decommissioned-leg-verified-by-skipped-markers]].
- **Sleep, not the scripts, is the failure mode.** The Mac slept at 3:45 PM; GPS ran on time at 16:32, but Perch and VALD only crept forward during short background wakes and did not finish until ~17:36–17:39. Perch timed out twice before try 3 succeeded. This is the same root cause as the earlier 6:30 AM GPS problem.
- **Retries saved the run but do not make it reliable** — the correct framing is "late, not missing," and the revisit trigger was set accordingly: reconsider only if GPS data goes *missing*, not merely late.
- **The `pmset` wake was recommended on 9/21 and declined on 9/22.** The 9/21 closeout listed `sudo pmset repeat wakeorpoweron MTWRFSU 16:28:00` as the recommended option and left it unset; the next morning Option 2 (leave sleep alone) was chosen instead. Both the enable command and its undo, `sudo pmset repeat cancel`, are recorded in `DataBase_GPS_Reporting/docs/STATUS.md`.
- **Windows VALD was already off.** The disabled step 1 in `refresh_all_data.bat` *is* the VALD step, and the Windows VALD pull had been broken since 8/2 — so the migration inherited a dead leg rather than duplicating a working one.
- **No alerts fired, so the Perch and VALD failure-alert paths remain unproven** — a successful-but-late run exercises neither the alert nor the absence of one.
- **Two writers would mean two mismatched databases**, so the Windows GPS writer was marked stopped (per Eric's report; not verifiable from the Mac), and the unused copy at `FA2026/_Mark_for_Deletion/gps_db_handoff_2026-09-21/` on Drive was queued for deletion.
- **The exposed VALD client secret was deliberately not rotated** — see [[concepts/deferred-credential-rotation-recorded-rationale]].

## Details

The substantive insight is that a scheduled job on a laptop has an execution precondition the scheduler does not enforce: the machine must be awake. macOS will grant short background wakes that let a long-running pull inch forward without ever giving it a contiguous window, which is why Perch timed out twice and both late jobs finished in a ragged ~17:36–17:39 cluster rather than at a clean retry boundary. From the outside, every observable signal is healthy — exit code 0, data current to 9/21, retries doing their job — and only the timestamp reveals that the schedule is not actually being honored. This is the same shape as the `Ready`-forever triggerless task in [[concepts/windows-backup-task-trigger-gotchas]] and the sleeping-laptop-misses-fixed-time-trigger gotcha recorded there: the scheduling layer reports truthfully about its own narrow predicate while the operational question (did this run when it was supposed to?) goes unanswered. The generalized version is catalogued in [[connections/the-execution-context-silently-edits-the-work-set]] — session lifetime, mount state, and now sleep state all shrink or delay what a run attempts without producing an error.

The `pmset` question is worth recording as a decision that was deliberated across two sessions rather than as a single call. The 9/21 closeout, written immediately after observing the hour-late finishes, listed the daily wake as the recommended fix; the 9/22 review declined it and attached a falsifiable revisit trigger instead. The reasoning for the reversal is that forcing a daily wake at 16:28 would make the afternoon pulls punctual at the cost of waking the machine every day for a job whose output is consumed the following morning anyway, so lateness inside a single day is not a defect in the consuming workflow. The condition that *would* justify the wake — data going missing rather than arriving late — is narrower and falsifiable, which keeps the deferral from decaying into an unexamined default. Storing the undo command alongside the enable command in the repo's own `STATUS.md` is the mechanism that makes the choice cheap to reverse regardless of which way it was decided.

Two ancillary findings deserve attention. First, the failure-alert paths for Perch and VALD have still never been exercised: a run that is late but ultimately successful produces no alert and therefore proves nothing about whether an alert would fire on a genuine failure. That leaves the alerting path in the same unverified state described in [[connections/alerting-path-must-not-share-the-monitored-systems-budget]] — untested alerting is indistinguishable from broken alerting. Second, the single-writer rule for the GPS database is a correctness constraint, not a tidiness preference: two machines writing the same database produce two divergent copies, and the Windows job being stopped is asserted rather than verified because the Mac has no way to inspect Windows' scheduler. The spare GPS database copy on Drive was queued for deletion for the same reason — a duplicate database is a future source of confusion about which one is authoritative. The cutover's durable record was fanned out to four repositories' `STATUS.md` files plus a handoff note at `~/.claude/global-memory/handoffs/2026-09-21-mac-owns-data-pulls.md`, a placement pattern examined in [[connections/write-the-decision-where-each-consumer-will-look]].

# Archive and Clear .errors.log Only After a Verified Clean Run

In the 2026-09-15 `/backup` session, the `.errors.log` was archived and cleared **only after** a re-run completed with 0 errors and 86 jobs — not after the individual fixes were applied. The sequence was: diagnose four errors, fix all four, re-run to a clean result, then archive and clear, then push. This ordering makes the clear an assertion backed by evidence rather than an assertion of intent.

## Key Points

- **The clear is a claim about current state,** so it must be preceded by a fresh observation of that state, not by the belief that the fixes worked.
- **Fixing and verifying are different events.** Four fixes were applied (two merges, one stale-directory move, one manifest addition); only the clean 86-job re-run established that all four took effect together.
- **`.errors.log` is an escalation channel, not a state record** — the standing discipline that entries must be confirmed stale before removal, here satisfied by an independent clean run rather than by reasoning.
- **The archive-then-clear step retains the evidence,** so a later question about what the four errors were remains answerable.
- **The clear also silences the session-start HOOK FAILURE warning,** which is why premature clearing is tempting: the nag is immediate and the verification is not.

## Details

The discipline in [[concepts/stale-error-log-archival-discipline]] establishes *that* entries must be confirmed stale against an independent source before clearing. This session supplies the operational ordering for the common case where the operator has just fixed the errors themselves: the independent source is a fresh run, and the fixes do not count as their own confirmation. The distinction matters because a multi-error run has cross-dependencies that reasoning can miss. Here, two of the four errors (merge-needed repos) were fixed by pushing, one (the rsync type-change failure) by moving stale directories aside, and one (the manifest gap) by editing and committing the manifest — and the manifest edit itself produced new work for the next run. A clear issued after the last fix would have been asserting that four independently-applied changes composed correctly, which is precisely the composition that [[connections/every-layer-reported-healthy-except-the-destination]] shows cannot be assumed from per-stage success.

The temptation to clear early comes from the asymmetry of feedback. The stale entry produces a visible HOOK FAILURE warning at every session start, so it is a continuous small cost, while the verification run is a discrete larger one. That asymmetry reliably pushes toward clearing on the strength of intent, which converts the log from a record of unresolved conditions into a record of conditions the operator *believed* resolved — the exact degradation that makes an escalation channel untrustworthy.

The archive half of the step carries its own known hazard. As documented in [[concepts/error-log-archive-collision-overwrite]], a date-keyed archive path destroyed three prior log lines when a second clear happened on the same day; the archive is only a safety net if its name cannot collide. In this session the archive preceded the clear and the run was the day's only clear, so the net held — but the general form of the rule is that both halves need verification: verify the run before clearing, and verify the archive landed before trusting it as the record.
